job.style: a clear textbook explanation with one worked example

passage: Numbers have special properties that help us understand them better. A factor is a number that divides another number exactly without leaving a remainder. For example, the factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12. Notice that both 1 and the number itself are always included as factors. Prime numbers are special because they have exactly two factors: 1 and the number itself. The number 2 is the smallest and only even prime number. Conversely, composite numbers have more than two factors. The number 1 is neither prime nor composite because it has only one factor. Multiples are found by multiplying a number by 1, 2, 3, and so on; since this sequence never ends, a number has an infinite amount of multiples. To check if a number is divisible by 3, we add all its digits together; if the sum is divisible by 3, the original number is also divisible by 3. For instance, 123 is divisible by 3 because 1+2+3 equals 6, which is a multiple of 3. Finally, the Highest Common Factor (HCF) is the largest factor shared by two numbers, while the Least Common Multiple (LCM) is the smallest non-zero multiple shared by them. These rules help us classify and organize numbers efficiently.

items.evidence: Notice that both 1 and the number itself are always included as factors.
items.q: Which list shows all the factors of 15?
items.explain: 1 and the number itself are always factors, so 15 has factors 1, 3, 5 and 15.

items.evidence: The number 2 is the smallest and only even prime number.
items.q: Sonu says even numbers can never be prime. Which number proves him wrong?
items.explain: 2 is the smallest prime and the only even prime, so not every even number is non-prime.

wrong.why: thinks small even numbers are prime
picks the example number from the passage

items.evidence: The number 1 is neither prime nor composite because it has only one factor.
items.q: Why is the number 1 not called a prime number?
options: It has just one factor, itself
It has no factors at all
It has many factors, so it is composite
It has two equal factors, 1 and 1
items.explain: A prime needs exactly two factors, but 1 has only one factor, so it is not prime.

wrong.why: thinks 1 is too small to have factors
counts 1 twice so it seems to have two factors

items.evidence: Multiples are found by multiplying a number by 1, 2, 3, and so on; since this sequence never ends, a number has an infinite amount of multiples.
items.q: Asha keeps writing multiples of 7 after 70. When will she reach the last one?
options: She never will, since they never end
She already has, since they stop at 70
She will at 84, since they stop at 7 × 12
She will at 700, since they stop at 7 × 100
items.explain: We can keep multiplying by 1, 2, 3 and so on forever, so multiples never end.

wrong.why: thinks multiples stop at the tenth, like a table
thinks multiples stop where school tables end
thinks multiples stop at a big round number

items.evidence: To check if a number is divisible by 3, we add all its digits together; if the sum is divisible by 3, the original number is also divisible by 3.
items.q: How can Raju check whether 471 is divisible by 3?
options: Add its digits 4, 7, 1 and check the sum
See if its last digit 1 is divisible by 3
See if its first digit 4 is divisible by 3
Multiply its digits 4, 7, 1 and check the product
items.explain: Add the digits: 4+7+1 = 12, which is divisible by 3, so 471 is too.

wrong.why: checks only the last digit, like the rule for 2
looks at a single digit instead of all digits
remembers using all digits but multiplies instead of adding
